Tutorial for spatial domain aware generation of semi-synthetic spatial transcriptomics data¶

Preliminaries and data loading¶

In [1]:
import pandas as pd
import anndata
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import warnings

(Optionally) download the single-nucleus dataset published by Langlieb et al. from braincelldata.org.

Alternatively, we are here providing a subset of this dataset containing five cell types:

In [2]:
celltypes_df = pd.read_csv("celltypes.csv", index_col=0)
celltypes_df

Quick start guide¶

"Blank" samples can be used as a starting point for downstream perturbations.

In our framework, this corresponds to samples generated at single-cell resolution, with all genes measured in the single-nucleus RNA-seq assay and no artificial increase in sparsity. All domains are defined transcriptionally by one cell type.

The following cell generates a sample of shape "moons":

In [4]:
from define_experiments import generate_blank_experiment
counts_df, coords_df, labels = generate_blank_experiment(adata=adata, 
                                                         regioncolname=regioncolname, 
                                                         celltypes_df=celltypes_df, 
                                                         shape="moons")

We can visualise this sample by a simple scatterplot of the labels:

In [5]:
plt.scatter(x=coords_df["x"], y=coords_df["y"], s=3, c=labels)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal')
plt.show()

If we want to visualise the count matrix, we can utilise PCA (or UMAPs, making sure not to over-interpret any results):

In [6]:
def plot_pca_and_umap(counts_df, coords_df, labels):
    import scanpy as sc
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")  # don't show ImplicitModificationWarning about string indices
        adata_moons = sc.AnnData(X=counts_df.reset_index(drop=True), 
                                obs=coords_df.join(labels.astype('str')))
    print("Generated adata")
    sc.pp.normalize_total(adata_moons)
    print("Normalized data")
    sc.pp.log1p(adata_moons)
    print("Log-transformed data")
    sc.pp.pca(adata_moons)  # this should take under a minute
    print("Calculated PCA")
    sc.pl.pca(adata_moons, color="label")
    plt.show()
    sc.pp.neighbors(adata_moons)
    print("Calculated neighborhood graph")
    sc.tl.umap(adata_moons)
    print("Calculated UMAP")
    sc.pl.umap(adata_moons, color="label")
    plt.show()
plot_pca_and_umap(counts_df, coords_df, labels)

To this blank sample, a range of different perturbations can now be applied.

Varying technological parameters¶

Resolution¶

First, we can modify the resolution of the previously generated blank sample, by binning cells into larger spot sizes.

In [7]:
from define_experiments import modify_resolution
modified_counts, modified_coords, modified_labels = modify_resolution(counts=counts_df, 
                                                                      coords=coords_df, 
                                                                      labels=labels, 
                                                                      gridlength=4  # this parameter controls bin size
                                                                      )

Visualising the new sample:

In [8]:
plt.scatter(x=modified_coords["x"], y=modified_coords["y"], s=30, c=modified_labels)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal')
plt.show()
In [9]:
plot_pca_and_umap(modified_counts, modified_coords, modified_labels)

Sparsity¶

We can further increase the sparsity in the sample to a user-specified target sparsity. The minimum sparsity possible (84%) is given by the sparsity of the single-nucleus data:

In [11]:
min_sparsity = (counts_df==0).sum().sum() / (counts_df.shape[0]*counts_df.shape[1])
print(f'sparsity of blank semi-synthetic sample: {min_sparsity:.4f}')

sparsity of blank semi-synthetic sample: 0.8367
In [12]:
from define_experiments import modify_sparsity
display(counts_df)
modified_counts, modified_coords, modified_labels = modify_sparsity(counts=counts_df, 
                                                                    coords=coords_df, 
                                                                    labels=labels, 
                                                                    goalprop=0.95  # this parameter controls goal sparsity
                                                                    )
display(modified_counts)

Generating samples with "perturbed" counts¶

Beside the possibility of perturbing existing "blank" samples, we implement two different count perturbation types (type I and type II) which are applied directly during the sample generation process.

Perturbation type I generates a sample with more similar gene expression between the different domains, while perturbation type II inserts a level of "noise cells" within the domains. For details, please refer to the methods section of our manuscript.

In [ ]:
from define_experiments import counts_perturbation_type1
counts_type1, coords_type1, labels_type1 = counts_perturbation_type1(adata=adata, 
                                                                     regioncolname=regioncolname, 
                                                                     celltypes_df=celltypes_df, 
                                                                     shape="moons", 
                                                                     noise_proportion=0.5)
In [14]:
plot_pca_and_umap(counts_type1, coords_type1, labels_type1)

Generating samples with varying domain sizes and shapes¶

In order to evaluate the effect of domain size, we can generate samples with varying domain thicknesses:

In [17]:
from define_experiments import vary_thickness
counts1, coords1, labels1 = vary_thickness(adata, regioncolname, celltypes_df, divides=(30, 60))
counts2, coords2, labels2 = vary_thickness(adata, regioncolname, celltypes_df, divides=(45, 50))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(ncols=2)
axes[0].scatter(x=coords1["x"], y=coords1["y"], s=2, c=labels1)
axes[0].set_aspect('equal')
axes[1].scatter(x=coords2["x"], y=coords2["y"], s=2, c=labels2)
axes[1].set_aspect('equal')
plt.show()

And finally, we implement a variety of shapes:

In [18]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(ncols=5, figsize=(10, 5), layout='constrained')
from tqdm import tqdm 
for shape, ax in tqdm(zip(['stripes', 'moons', 'circles', 'blobs', 'varied'], axes), total=5): 
    counts_df, coords_df, labels = generate_blank_experiment(adata=adata, 
                                                             regioncolname=regioncolname, 
                                                             celltypes_df=celltypes_df, 
                                                             shape=shape)
    ax.scatter(x=coords_df["x"], y=coords_df["y"], s=2, c=labels)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
plt.show()

100%|██████████| 5/5 [00:13<00:00,  2.66s/it]

In order to enable unbiased evaluation of shape effects, we provide an interface for creating samples with different permutations of label-to-cell type assignments.

In [19]:
from define_experiments import vary_shapes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(ncols=5, figsize=(10, 5), layout='constrained')
from tqdm import tqdm 
for shape, ax in tqdm(zip(['stripes', 'moons', 'circles', 'blobs', 'varied'], axes), total=5): 
    permutation = "1324"  # default: "1234"
    n_domains = 4 if shape in ['stripes', 'blobs', 'varied'] else 3
    permutation = permutation[:n_domains]
    counts_df, coords_df, labels = vary_shapes(adata=adata, 
                                               regioncolname=regioncolname, 
                                               celltypes_df=celltypes_df, 
                                               shape=shape, 
                                               permutation=permutation)
    ax.scatter(x=coords_df["x"], y=coords_df["y"], s=2, c=labels)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
plt.show()
